subject: history
key_question: What is the legacy of Ancient Egypt?
challenge: Our challenge is to create a museum exhibition about Ancient Egypt.

writing_outcome.description: A non-chronological report about Ancient Egypt

enquiry_outcome: Museum exhibition display — annotated artefacts, maps, and pupil-written information cards

lessons.what: About the geography and society of Ancient Egypt
lessons.why: understanding where Egypt is and how it was organised helps us explore why this civilisation became so powerful
lessons.success: locating Egypt on a map and describing at least three features of Egyptian society

vocabulary.definition: A large group of people who live together and share a language, laws and way of life.
The ruler of Ancient Egypt, believed by Egyptians to be a god as well as a king.
The longest river in Africa, which runs through Egypt and gave Ancient Egyptians water, food and transport.

slides.title: Where in the World is Egypt?
slides.content: Egypt is in North Africa. It sits on the banks of the River Nile, which flows north into the Mediterranean Sea. Most Egyptian settlements were along the Nile because the surrounding land was desert.

slides.title: Reading a Map Together
slides.content: Look at the map of Ancient Egypt. Find the River Nile, the Mediterranean Sea, the Sahara Desert and the Red Sea. What do you notice about where Egyptians chose to build their cities?

slides.title: What Do We Already Know?
slides.content: Discuss in trios: What do you already know about Ancient Egypt? Share one idea each. What would you LIKE to find out?

lessons.what: When Ancient Egypt existed and how long it lasted
lessons.why: placing Egypt in time helps us understand how old this civilisation was and how it compares to other periods we have studied
lessons.success: placing at least four key Egyptian periods on a timeline and using dates correctly

vocabulary.definition: A series of rulers from the same family, one after another.
Before Christ — used for dates that come before the year 0. The bigger the number, the longer ago it was.
A line that shows events in the order they happened, with dates to show when.

quiz.question: In which continent is Egypt located?
quiz.answer: Africa

quiz.question: What do we call the ruler of Ancient Egypt?
quiz.answer: Pharaoh

quiz.question: Which great river was central to Egyptian life?
quiz.answer: The River Nile

slides.title: The Timeline of Ancient Egypt
slides.content: Ancient Egypt lasted for over 3000 years — from around 3100 BC to 30 BC. It was divided into periods called dynasties. The Old Kingdom (2686–2181 BC) is when the great pyramids were built. The New Kingdom (1550–1069 BC) is when famous pharaohs like Tutankhamun and Ramesses II ruled.

slides.title: Building Our Class Timeline
slides.content: Let's place key events on our class timeline. We will add: the first pharaoh (3100 BC), the building of the Great Pyramid (2560 BC), Tutankhamun's reign (1332 BC), and the end of Ancient Egypt (30 BC).

slides.title: Order the Dynasties
slides.content: Cut out the dynasty cards and place them in order on your timeline. Write the correct dates next to each one. Challenge: which dynasty lasted the longest?

lessons.what: How Egyptian society was organised, from the pharaoh to the peasants
lessons.why: understanding the social hierarchy shows us how power worked in Ancient Egypt and why so few people held so much control
lessons.success: ordering the levels of Egyptian society correctly and explaining the role of at least two different groups

vocabulary.definition: A system where people are ranked in order of power or importance, from the most powerful at the top to the least powerful at the bottom.
A person who could read and write and kept records for the pharaoh. Scribes were important because most people could not read.
A poor farmer who worked the land. Most people in Ancient Egypt were peasants.

quiz.question: What is a dynasty?
quiz.answer: A series of rulers from the same family

quiz.question: What does BC mean?
quiz.answer: Before Christ — dates before the year 0

quiz.question: Approximately when was the Great Pyramid built?
quiz.answer: Around 2560 BC (during the Old Kingdom)

slides.title: The Pyramid of Egyptian Society
slides.content: Egyptian society was shaped like a pyramid. At the top was the pharaoh — one person with total power. Below were priests and nobles, then soldiers, then craftsmen and scribes, and at the bottom the peasants — the largest group of all.

slides.title: Ranking the Roles
slides.content: Here are eight role cards. Together, let's place them on our hierarchy diamond. We'll discuss: who held the most power? Who did the most work? Who had the least choice about their life?

slides.title: Where Would You Have Been?
slides.content: Look at the descriptions of each group. Which level of society would most people in our class have belonged to? Write three sentences explaining who you would have been and what your life would have been like.

lessons.what: What Ancient Egyptians believed about gods, death and the afterlife
lessons.why: understanding Egyptian beliefs helps us explain why they built pyramids, mummified bodies and created so much religious art
lessons.success: naming at least three Egyptian gods and explaining why Egyptians believed in the afterlife

vocabulary.definition: Believing in more than one god. Ancient Egyptians worshipped over 2000 different gods and goddesses.
A process of preserving a dead body by drying it out so it would last for thousands of years.
The life that Egyptians believed came after death. They thought the soul would live on if the body was preserved.

quiz.question: What do we call the system that ranks people by power, with the pharaoh at the top?
quiz.answer: Hierarchy

quiz.question: What job did a scribe do?
quiz.answer: They could read and write, and kept records for the pharaoh

quiz.question: Which group made up most of the Egyptian population?
quiz.answer: Peasants (farmers)

slides.title: Egyptian Gods and Goddesses
slides.content: Ancient Egyptians believed in over 2000 gods. Ra was the sun god and king of the gods. Osiris ruled the afterlife. Anubis watched over mummification. Isis was the goddess of magic and motherhood. Each god had a role in explaining the world around them.

slides.title: Reading About the Afterlife
slides.content: Let's read together about what Egyptians believed happened after death. They thought the heart was weighed against a feather — if it was light, the soul entered the afterlife. If it was heavy with wrongdoing, it was eaten by a monster called Ammit.

slides.title: Why Did Egyptians Mummify?
slides.content: Discuss in trios: why was mummification so important to Ancient Egyptians? How does this connect to their belief in the afterlife? Share your ideas with the class.

lessons.what: The architectural and engineering achievements of Ancient Egypt
lessons.why: studying what Egyptians built shows us how advanced their civilisation was and why it has lasted as a legacy for thousands of years
lessons.success: describing at least two Egyptian achievements and explaining what they tell us about Egyptian society

vocabulary.definition: A huge stone building with a square base and four triangular sides, built as a tomb for a pharaoh.
A statue with a human head and a lion's body. The Great Sphinx at Giza is one of the largest statues in the world.
A person who designs buildings and structures. Egyptian architects planned enormous building projects without modern tools.

quiz.question: What is polytheism?
quiz.answer: Believing in more than one god

quiz.question: Name one Egyptian god and what they were god of.
quiz.answer: Any correct answer, e.g. Ra — sun god; Osiris — afterlife; Anubis — mummification

quiz.question: What happened to the heart of the dead in Egyptian belief?
quiz.answer: It was weighed against a feather to decide if the soul could enter the afterlife

slides.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
slides.content: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC for Pharaoh Khufu. It is made of about 2.3 million stone blocks, each weighing between 2.5 and 15 tonnes. For 3800 years it was the tallest human-made structure in the world. Historians still debate exactly how it was built.

slides.title: How Were the Pyramids Built?
slides.content: Look at three different theories about how the pyramids were constructed. Which theory do you think is most convincing? What evidence would you need to be sure?

slides.title: Egyptian Achievements — Fact File
slides.content: Choose one achievement from the word bank (pyramid, obelisk, irrigation system, hieroglyphics, calendar). Research using your fact cards and write five key facts. Be ready to share with the class.

lessons.what: The different types of sources that tell us about Ancient Egypt
lessons.why: historians can only know about the past through the evidence left behind, so understanding source types is essential to studying history
lessons.success: identifying at least three types of historical source and explaining what each one can and cannot tell us

vocabulary.definition: An object made or used by people in the past. Artefacts help historians understand how people lived.
The Ancient Egyptian writing system, made up of pictures and symbols. It was decoded in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone.
A stone discovered in 1799 with the same message written in three scripts. It allowed historians to decode Egyptian hieroglyphics.

quiz.question: What is a pyramid?
quiz.answer: A huge stone building with a square base and four triangular sides, built as a tomb for a pharaoh

quiz.question: What is a sphinx?
quiz.answer: A statue with a human head and lion's body

quiz.question: Name one thing that makes the Great Pyramid remarkable.
quiz.answer: Any valid answer, e.g. built from 2.3 million stone blocks; tallest building in the world for 3800 years

slides.title: Types of Historical Source
slides.content: Historians use many types of source: written documents (like papyrus scrolls), artefacts (like pottery and jewellery), images (like tomb paintings), buildings (like temples and tombs), and oral accounts. Each source gives us different clues about the past.

slides.title: Analysing an Artefact
slides.content: Look at this image of an artefact from Ancient Egypt. Using the source analysis frames, answer: What is it? Who might have made it? What does it tell us about Egyptian life? What can it NOT tell us?

slides.title: Source Detectives
slides.content: You have four different sources about Ancient Egypt. Sort them into types. For each, write one thing it tells us and one question it leaves unanswered.

lessons.what: How to compare two sources and identify similarities, differences and limitations
lessons.why: no single source tells the whole story — historians compare multiple sources to build a more complete picture of the past
lessons.success: comparing two sources and identifying at least one similarity, one difference and one limitation of each

vocabulary.definition: Something made or written at the time of the events it shows — for example, a tomb painting made in Ancient Egypt.
Something written or created about the past by someone who was not there — for example, a textbook written today about Ancient Egypt.
When a source only tells part of the story, or shows things in a way that favours one side. A pharaoh's own account of a battle might be biased.

quiz.question: What is an artefact?
quiz.answer: An object made or used by people in the past

quiz.question: What are hieroglyphics?
quiz.answer: The Ancient Egyptian writing system, made up of pictures and symbols

quiz.question: What was the Rosetta Stone?
quiz.answer: A stone with the same message in three scripts, which allowed historians to decode hieroglyphics

slides.title: Daily Life — What the Sources Show
slides.content: Two sources about the same event can look very different. Source A is a painting from inside a tomb showing a wealthy family at a banquet. Source B is a list of food rations recorded by a scribe for pyramid workers. Both tell us about food — but they tell very different stories about who ate well.

slides.title: Comparing Two Sources
slides.content: Look at Sources A and B together. Fill in the comparison grid: What does each source show? What do they agree on? Where do they differ? Why might they be different? What can each NOT tell us?

slides.title: Does the Source Agree?
slides.content: Read the claim: 'Ancient Egyptians ate well and had plenty of food.' Use Sources A and B to argue FOR and AGAINST this claim. Write two sentences for each side, then give your verdict.

lessons.what: Why Ancient Egypt became so powerful, through trade, agriculture and military strength
lessons.why: understanding the causes of Egypt's power helps us see how civilisations grow — and connects to the idea that geography shapes history
lessons.success: explaining at least two reasons why Egypt became powerful and giving an example for each

vocabulary.definition: A path along which goods are carried and exchanged between different places. Egypt controlled important routes connecting Africa, Asia and the Mediterranean.
Farming — growing crops and raising animals for food. The flooding of the Nile made the land around it extremely fertile.
Defeating and taking control of another place or people. Some pharaohs expanded Egypt's empire through conquest.

quiz.question: What is a primary source?
quiz.answer: Something made or written at the time of the events it shows

quiz.question: What is a secondary source?
quiz.answer: Something written about the past by someone who was not there

quiz.question: What does bias mean in a historical source?
quiz.answer: When a source only tells part of the story or favours one side

slides.title: Why Was Egypt So Powerful?
slides.content: Egypt became powerful for three main reasons: geography (the Nile provided fertile farmland in the middle of desert, making Egypt rich in food), trade (Egypt controlled routes between Africa, Asia and the Mediterranean, trading gold, papyrus and linen), and military strength (strong armies under warrior pharaohs like Ramesses II expanded Egypt's territory).

slides.title: Mapping Egypt's Trade Routes
slides.content: Using the blank map, mark Egypt, the River Nile and the key trading partners. Draw arrows to show the direction of trade. What goods went IN to Egypt? What goods went OUT? What does this tell us about what Egypt was good at producing?

slides.title: Why Was Egypt Powerful? — The Debate
slides.content: In trios, each person argues for one factor: geography, trade, or military. Make your best case for WHY your factor was the most important. Then vote — which factor did your trio find most convincing?

lessons.what: Why Ancient Egypt declined and what legacy it left behind
lessons.why: studying the end of a civilisation is just as important as its rise — it helps us understand what makes societies fragile and what they leave behind
lessons.success: giving at least two reasons for Egypt's decline and identifying at least two parts of Egypt's legacy that still affect us today

vocabulary.definition: Something left behind by a person or civilisation that still affects us today. Egypt's legacy includes mathematics, medicine and architectural techniques.
When something becomes gradually less powerful or important over time. Ancient Egypt declined slowly over several centuries.
The last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. After her death in 30 BC, Egypt was absorbed into the Roman Empire.

quiz.question: What is a trade route?
quiz.answer: A path along which goods are carried and exchanged between different places

quiz.question: Why was the River Nile so important to Egyptian agriculture?
quiz.answer: Its annual floods left behind fertile silt that made the surrounding land ideal for farming

quiz.question: Name one warrior pharaoh who expanded Egypt's empire.
quiz.answer: Ramesses II (or any other valid answer)

slides.title: The Fall of Ancient Egypt
slides.content: Egypt declined for several reasons: invasions from Assyrians, Persians, Greeks and finally Romans; internal conflict and power struggles between pharaohs and priests; climate change reducing Nile floods; and economic strain from costly building projects. In 30 BC, after Cleopatra's death, Egypt became a Roman province and the era of the pharaohs ended.

slides.title: Which Factor Mattered Most?
slides.content: Here are five causes of Egypt's decline. On your ranking diamond, place them from most important (top) to least important (bottom). Discuss: is there a single cause, or did these factors work together?

slides.title: Legacy or Not?
slides.content: Read the list of modern things that have Egyptian origins: the 365-day calendar, surgical instruments, toothpaste, paper (papyrus), and the concept of school examinations. For each one, write one sentence explaining the connection to Ancient Egypt. Which surprises you most?

lessons.what: The features of a non-chronological report and how historians write about Ancient Egypt
lessons.why: studying a model text shows us what good historical writing looks like before we attempt our own report
lessons.success: identifying at least four features of a non-chronological report in the model text and explaining what each one does

vocabulary.definition: A type of writing that gives information about a topic. It does not follow time order — sections are organised by theme instead.
The opening part of a piece of writing that tells the reader what it will be about and why it is interesting.
A title used inside a piece of writing to show that a new section or theme is starting.

quiz.question: What is a legacy?
quiz.answer: Something left behind by a civilisation or person that still affects us today

quiz.question: In what year did Ancient Egypt end?
quiz.answer: 30 BC

quiz.question: Name one reason for Egypt's decline.
quiz.answer: Any valid answer, e.g. invasions from Assyrians/Persians/Greeks/Romans; internal power struggles; climate change; expensive building projects

slides.title: Reading a Non-Chronological Report
slides.content: A non-chronological report has a clear structure: an introduction that hooks the reader, themed sections each with a subheading, technical vocabulary used correctly, the present tense for facts that are still true, and a conclusion that links back to the main idea. Let's read the model text together and spot these features.

slides.title: What Makes a Good Report?
slides.content: Using the model text, work in pairs to find: one strong introduction sentence; one technical word used well; one subheading that tells you exactly what the section is about; one fact that surprised you. Highlight and annotate your copy.

slides.title: Annotating the Model Text
slides.content: On your own copy of the model text, label: introduction, subheadings, technical vocabulary (circle in blue), present tense verbs (underline in red), connectives (box in green). Count how many you find of each type.

lessons.what: How to plan a non-chronological report and an exhibition display
lessons.why: planning carefully before writing means our finished report will be more organised, detailed and interesting for our readers
lessons.success: completing a planning frame with four section headings and at least two key facts for each section

vocabulary.definition: A collection of objects, images or displays put together for people to look at and learn from.
A person who is in charge of choosing what goes in a museum or exhibition and how it is arranged.
A part of a report that focuses on one theme or aspect of the topic, introduced by a subheading.

quiz.question: What is a non-chronological report?
quiz.answer: A type of writing that gives information organised by theme, not time order

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a subheading?
quiz.answer: To introduce a new section and tell the reader what it is about

quiz.question: Name two features of a good introduction.
quiz.answer: Any two valid answers, e.g. hooks the reader; introduces the topic; tells the reader what to expect; uses an interesting fact or question

slides.title: Planning Our Report and Exhibition
slides.content: Our report will have five sections: Who were the Ancient Egyptians? (geography and society) / What did they believe? (gods and afterlife) / What did they achieve? (pyramids and architecture) / How do we know? (sources and evidence) / What is their legacy? (impact on the modern world). Each section will also become part of our museum display.

slides.title: What Will We Include?
slides.content: Look at the planning grid together. For the first two sections, let's brainstorm: what do we know? What questions can we answer? What images, artefacts or facts would work well in an exhibition? I'll model how to complete the grid for Section 1.

slides.title: My Exhibition Plan
slides.content: Complete your planning grid for all five sections. For each section: write the subheading; note 2–3 key facts; note one image or artefact that would work well; write one question your display panel should answer.

lessons.what: How to write sections of a non-chronological report using evidence from our research
lessons.why: turning our notes and research into a piece of extended writing is the moment where our knowledge becomes a real product that others can read and learn from
lessons.success: writing at least two complete paragraphs that include a subheading, a topic sentence, two supporting facts and a concluding sentence

vocabulary.definition: A group of sentences that are all about the same idea, separated from the next paragraph by a new line.
A word that joins ideas together in a sentence. Examples: because, although, which, when, however.
When the ideas in a piece of writing link together clearly, so the reader can follow the argument from one sentence to the next.

quiz.question: What is an exhibition?
quiz.answer: A collection of objects or displays put together for people to look at and learn from

quiz.question: What does a curator do?
quiz.answer: They choose what goes in a museum or exhibition and how it is arranged

quiz.question: How many sections will our report have?
quiz.answer: Five sections

slides.title: Shared Write — Geography of Egypt
slides.content: Let me model writing the first section together. Topic sentence: 'Ancient Egypt was built on one of the most extraordinary geographical features in the world — the River Nile.' Now I'll add two supporting facts, use a conjunction to link ideas, and write a sentence that brings us back to the big question: why did Egypt become a civilisation?

slides.title: Writing Together — Beliefs Section
slides.content: Using our planning notes, let's write the 'What did they believe?' section together. I'll start the first sentence — you suggest what comes next. We'll build the whole paragraph as a class, then read it back and check it makes sense.

slides.title: Independent Write — My Own Section
slides.content: Choose ONE section from your plan that you feel most confident about. Write it independently: subheading, topic sentence, two supporting facts (with evidence), a conjunction, and a closing sentence. Use the model text to check your structure as you write.

lessons.what: How to edit and improve a draft, and how to present information for a museum display
lessons.why: editing is where good writing becomes great writing — historians and writers always redraft, and our museum visitors deserve the best version of our work
lessons.success: making at least three improvements to a peer's draft using the editing checklist, and completing one display panel ready for the exhibition

vocabulary.definition: To read through writing carefully and make improvements — fixing mistakes, adding detail, improving vocabulary or changing the order of ideas.
The people who will read or watch your work. Our audience is museum visitors who want to learn about Ancient Egypt.
The way words and images are arranged on a page or display. Good layout makes information easier to read and more interesting.

quiz.question: What is a paragraph?
quiz.answer: A group of sentences all about the same idea

quiz.question: Give an example of a conjunction.
quiz.answer: Because / although / when / however / which (any valid example)

quiz.question: What does cohesion mean in writing?
quiz.answer: When ideas in a piece of writing link together clearly so the reader can follow them

slides.title: Editing Checklist — What to Look For
slides.content: When editing, check: Does each paragraph have a clear topic? Are facts accurate? Are conjunctions used to link ideas? Is vocabulary precise and varied? Does each section end with a sentence that links back to the key question? I'll model using the checklist on a sample paragraph.

slides.title: Peer Editing
slides.content: Swap your draft with a partner. Using the editing checklist, read their work and suggest three improvements. Use the code: V = vocabulary change / F = missing fact / S = structure change. Write your suggestions on a sticky note. Discuss your feedback together.

slides.title: Final Edits and Display Panel
slides.content: Make the improvements suggested by your partner. Then transfer your best section to your museum display panel: write your subheading in large letters, copy your paragraph neatly, and add one image or artefact annotation. Your display must be ready for exhibition day.

lessons.what: How to present our learning to an audience and reflect on what we have learned about Ancient Egypt
lessons.why: sharing our enquiry work is how historians communicate their findings — and reflecting helps us understand what we have learned and what we could do differently next time
lessons.success: presenting one display panel to visitors and writing three sentences of honest reflection about what they have learned and what surprised them

vocabulary.definition: Thinking carefully about what you have done, what went well, what was difficult and what you would do differently.
The part you played in a shared project. Every member of the class contributed something to our museum exhibition.
Someone who studies and writes about the past, using evidence and sources to build up a picture of how people lived.

quiz.question: What does it mean to edit a piece of writing?
quiz.answer: To read it carefully and make improvements — fixing mistakes, adding detail, improving vocabulary

quiz.question: Who is the audience for our museum exhibition?
quiz.answer: Museum visitors who want to learn about Ancient Egypt

quiz.question: What is layout?
quiz.answer: The way words and images are arranged on a page or display to make information easier to read

slides.title: How to Present at a Museum
slides.content: A good museum guide: welcomes visitors and tells them what the display is about; explains the most interesting things rather than reading everything aloud; uses technical vocabulary correctly; invites questions. Let me model a 60-second introduction to our Egypt exhibition.

slides.title: Gallery Walk
slides.content: Spend 10 minutes walking around the exhibition as a visitor. Leave a sticky note on ONE display panel: one thing you learned and one question you still have. Then return to your own panel to answer any questions left for you.

slides.title: Reflection — What Have I Learned?
slides.content: In your book, write three sentences: one thing you know NOW that you did not know at the start of this enquiry; one source or artefact that changed how you thought about Egypt; and your answer to the key question — what IS the legacy of Ancient Egypt?
